stem: Simeon's song when he takes the child Jesus in the Temple (Luke 2:29–32, the Nunc Dimittis: "Now thou dost dismiss thy servant, O Lord") is said every day in which hour of the Liturgy of the Hours?
options: Morning Prayer (Lauds)
Evening Prayer (Vespers)
Midday Prayer (Sext)
Night Prayer (Compline)
why: The Nunc Dimittis is the Gospel canticle of Night Prayer (Compline), just as Zachary's Benedictus belongs to Morning Prayer and Mary's Magnificat to Evening Prayer.
source: Luke 2:29–32; General Instruction of the Liturgy of the Hours 50

es.stem: El cántico de Simeón cuando toma en brazos al niño Jesús en el Templo (Lucas 2,29–32, el Nunc Dimittis: "Ahora, Señor, puedes dejar ir a tu siervo") se reza cada día en ¿cuál hora de la Liturgia de las Horas?
options: Oración de la mañana (Laudes)
Oración de la tarde (Vísperas)
Oración de mediodía (Sexta)
Oración de la noche (Completas)
es.why: El Nunc Dimittis es el cántico evangélico de la Oración de la noche (Completas), así como el Benedictus de Zacarías pertenece a Laudes y el Magníficat de María a Vísperas.

stem: On the road to Emmaus (Luke 24:13–35), two disciples walk for miles with the risen Jesus without knowing him. At what moment, Luke says, were their eyes opened so that they knew him?
options: in the breaking of the bread
when they saw the empty tomb
when he called them each by name
when he said, peace be to you
why: Luke 24:30–31, 35: at table he took bread, blessed, broke and gave it, "and their eyes were opened, and they knew him"; they tell the others he was known to them in the breaking of bread.

es.stem: En el camino de Emaús (Lucas 24,13–35), dos discípulos caminan kilómetros con Jesús resucitado sin reconocerlo. ¿En qué momento, según Lucas, se les abrieron los ojos y lo reconocieron?
options: en el momento de partir el pan
cuando vieron el sepulcro vacío
cuando los llamó por su nombre
al decirles: la paz con ustedes
es.why: Lucas 24,30–31.35: en la mesa tomó el pan, lo bendijo, lo partió y se lo dio, "y se les abrieron los ojos y lo reconocieron"; luego cuentan a los demás que lo reconocieron al partir el pan.

stem: In Jesus' parable of the Pharisee and the publican, the tax collector (Luke 18:9–14), which man "went down into his house justified," and on what ground?
options: the Pharisee, who fasted and tithed
the publican, who humbled himself
both, since each had gone to pray
neither, since both judged others
why: Luke 18:13–14: the publican, striking his breast, prayed "O God, be merciful to me a sinner"; he went home justified, "because every one that exalteth himself shall be humbled: and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted." The Catechism (CCC 2559, 2631) holds up his prayer as the model of humility.

es.stem: En la parábola de Jesús sobre el fariseo y el publicano, el cobrador de impuestos (Lucas 18,9–14), ¿cuál de los dos "bajó a su casa justificado", y por qué razón?
options: el fariseo, que ayunaba y daba el diezmo
el publicano, que se humilló ante Dios
los dos, porque los dos fueron a orar
ninguno, porque los dos juzgaban a otros
es.why: Lucas 18,13–14: el publicano, golpeándose el pecho, oró "Oh Dios, ten compasión de mí, que soy pecador"; volvió a su casa justificado, "porque todo el que se ensalza será humillado, y el que se humilla será ensalzado". El Catecismo (CIC 2559, 2631) presenta su oración como modelo de humildad.

stem: The Gospel of John calls Jesus' miracles "signs" (Greek semeia), beginning with water made wine at Cana, where he "manifested his glory" (John 2:11). Why does John use that word for them?
options: they were proofs given to satisfy the Pharisees
they foretold the Temple's coming destruction
they reveal his glory and lead to faith in him
they were acts he kept hidden from the crowds
why: John 2:11 and 20:30–31: the signs point past themselves to who Jesus is; at Cana "his disciples believed in him," and John says the signs were written "that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God." See CCC 547–548.

es.stem: El Evangelio de Juan llama "signos" (en griego semeia) a los milagros de Jesús, empezando por el agua convertida en vino en Caná, donde "manifestó su gloria" (Juan 2,11). ¿Por qué Juan usa esa palabra para ellos?
options: eran pruebas para dejar contentos a los fariseos
anunciaban la próxima destrucción del Templo
revelan su gloria y llevan a creer en él
eran actos que ocultaba a la multitud
es.why: Juan 2,11 y 20,30–31: los signos apuntan más allá de sí mismos, a quién es Jesús; en Caná "sus discípulos creyeron en él", y Juan dice que los signos se escribieron "para que crean que Jesús es el Cristo, el Hijo de Dios". Ver CIC 547–548.

stem: After the Resurrection, by the Sea of Galilee, Jesus asks Peter three times, "lovest thou me?" and each time gives him a charge: feed my lambs, feed my sheep (John 21:15–17). Since St. Augustine, why has the threefold question been explained?
options: to undo his three denials, one by one
to match the three days in the tomb
to echo the three tents Peter offered
to recall the three years of his ministry
why: John 21:15–17 answers Peter's three denials by a charcoal fire (John 18:17–27); Augustine wrote that the threefold confession answers the threefold denial. The Church also sees Peter given charge of the flock here (CCC 553, 881).
source: John 21:15–17; St. Augustine, Tractates on John 123.5; CCC 553, 881

es.stem: Después de la Resurrección, junto al mar de Galilea, Jesús le pregunta tres veces a Pedro "¿me amas?" y cada vez le da un encargo: apacienta mis corderos, apacienta mis ovejas (Juan 21,15–17). Desde san Agustín, ¿cómo se ha explicado la triple pregunta?
options: para reparar sus tres negaciones, una por una
para evocar los tres días en el sepulcro
para recordar las tres tiendas que Pedro ofreció
para recordar los tres años de su ministerio
es.why: Juan 21,15–17 responde a las tres negaciones de Pedro junto a un fuego de brasas (Juan 18,17–27); san Agustín escribió que la triple confesión responde a la triple negación. La Iglesia también ve aquí a Pedro recibiendo el cuidado del rebaño (CIC 553, 881).

stem: A family plans a dinner and, instead of the rich friends and relatives who would invite them back, asks people who could never host them in return. Which teaching of Jesus in Luke 14 are they following?
options: sit down in the lowest place at table
first count the cost before you build
be not anxious for what you shall eat
when you make a feast, call the poor
why: Luke 14:12–14: "when thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, and the blind; and thou shalt be blessed, because they have not wherewith to make thee recompense." The lowest place (14:7–11) is about seating, and counting the cost (14:28) about discipleship.

es.stem: Una familia organiza una cena y, en lugar de invitar a los amigos y parientes ricos que luego los invitarían a ellos, invita a personas que nunca podrían devolverles la invitación. ¿Qué enseñanza de Jesús en Lucas 14 están siguiendo?
options: siéntate en el último lugar de la mesa
calcula primero el costo antes de construir
no te inquietes por lo que vas a comer
cuando des un banquete, invita a los pobres
es.why: Lucas 14,12–14: "cuando des un banquete, invita a los pobres, a los lisiados, a los cojos y a los ciegos; y serás dichoso, porque ellos no tienen con qué pagarte". El último lugar (14,7–11) trata de dónde sentarse, y calcular el costo (14,28) trata del discipulado.

stem: In the Annunciation (Luke 1:26–38), how does Mary respond to the angel Gabriel's message that she will bear a son?
why: Mary first asks how this will happen, since she knows not man; Gabriel answers that the Holy Ghost will come upon her and nothing is impossible with God. She then consents: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word." The Church calls this her fiat (CCC 484, 494).

rubric.point: Says Mary consents or says yes, for example 'behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word', or names her fiat. Saying only that she was afraid or troubled does not count.

Mentions her question, how this can be since she knows not man (is a virgin), or Gabriel's answer that the Holy Spirit will overshadow her. Mentioning only that she was troubled at the greeting counts as partly.
Notes that her question is not doubt, unlike Zachary, who was struck silent, or that the Church calls her yes the fiat (optional, strengthens).

es.stem: En la Anunciación (Lucas 1,26–38), ¿cómo responde María al mensaje del ángel Gabriel de que dará a luz un hijo?
es.why: María primero pregunta cómo sucederá, pues no conoce varón; Gabriel le responde que el Espíritu Santo vendrá sobre ella y que para Dios nada es imposible. Entonces ella acepta: "He aquí la esclava del Señor; hágase en mí según tu palabra". La Iglesia llama a esto su fiat (CIC 484, 494).

stem: At the cross in John 19:25–27, what does Jesus say to his mother and to the disciple whom he loved, and how does the Catholic Church read the scene?
why: Jesus says to his mother, "Woman, behold thy son," and to the disciple, "Behold thy mother," and from that hour the disciple took her to his own. The Church reads it as Mary given as mother to all disciples, the mother of the Church (CCC 964, 2618; Lumen Gentium 58).

rubric.point: Gives the words or their sense: Jesus entrusts his mother to the disciple and the disciple to his mother ('Woman, behold thy son'; 'Behold thy mother'). Saying only that Jesus spoke to Mary, without the entrusting, does not count.
Says the Church sees Mary given as mother to all believers or to the Church, with the beloved disciple standing for every disciple. Saying only that John looked after her counts as partly.
Mentions that the disciple took her into his own home from that hour, or the echo of 'woman' at Cana (optional, strengthens).

es.stem: Junto a la cruz, en Juan 19,25–27, ¿qué les dice Jesús a su madre y al discípulo a quien amaba, y cómo lee la Iglesia católica esta escena?
es.why: Jesús le dice a su madre: "Mujer, ahí tienes a tu hijo", y al discípulo: "Ahí tienes a tu madre", y desde aquella hora el discípulo la recibió en su casa. La Iglesia lo lee como María entregada como madre a todos los discípulos, madre de la Iglesia (CIC 964, 2618; Lumen Gentium 58).
